newsitem.title: USA: Police rule out alleged Versace killer struck again.
newsitem.headline: Police rule out alleged Versace killer struck again.

text.p: Andrew Cunanan, the alleged multiple killer wanted in the July 15 slaying of fashion designer Gianni Versace, did not go on to kill a Miami doctor two days later as originally suspected, police said on Saturday.
Announcing an arrest in the Thursday strangling of Silvio Alfonso, police spokesman Denis Morales said: "The subject arrested is not Andrew Cunanan."
Alfonso was found dead in the bedroom of his Miami Springs home, just north of Miami's international airport.

FBI and police hunting Cunanan, described as a charming, gregarious homosexual prostitute, feared he might have struck again after a man described as resembling Cunanan was seen running from the scene.

The arrested man was named as Yosvany Hernandez, 28, a Cuban immigrant. Police said officers had noticed during voluntary questioning that he was wearing what appeared to be a watch and bracelet belonging to the dead man and had recently attempted to alter his appearance.
Police said on Saturday that they considered the Alfonso case to be closed.
A photograph released to media of Hernandez showed a passing resemblance to Cunanan, 27, who is wanted for the Versace killing and at least four other murders across the United States since April.
Cunanan is believed to have remained in south Florida, and was considered armed and dangerous. He has a $45,000 reward on his head.
Police raided a Miami Beach hotel late on Friday, taking away bags of evidence after the owner said Cunanan had stayed there for several weeks before the Versace killing.
She described him as having "a beautiful smile, and beautiful teeth."
The San Diego Union-Tribune reported on Saturday that Cunanan feared he might have contracted the AIDS virus and told a counsellor he would "get" whoever may have transmitted it to him.
Two months before he set out on his alleged cross-country murder spree, Cunanan approached Mike Dudley, a volunteer counsellor at a nonprofit agency for people with AIDS and HIV.

"He started asking me pretty basic questions about HIV transmission," Dudley told the newspaper. "He was mentioning some of the things he had done sexually. I explained the things were sort of in the gray area and he should take greater precautions."
Dudley said Cunanan grew angry during the conversation.
"He became agitated and he got up and kicked the wall and said, 'If I find out who did this to me, I'm gonna get them,'" Dudley said.
The newspaper said Cunanan never told Dudley whether he had tested positive for HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.
Police say they do not know if Cunanan and Versace ever had sexual contact. Vanity Fair writer Maureen Orth, who has researched Cunanan extensively, said they met at least once in San Francisco.

Versace was laid to rest on Friday in a cemetery overlooking Lake Como in Italy. His sister, Donatella, and brother, Santo, led about a dozen mourners into the secluded cemetery in Moultrasio village where the Italian designer had a villa.
Santo carried a gold casket containing the ashes of Versace, who was cremated on Thursday in Fort Lauderdale near Miami.
A memorial service was held for him on Friday at St. Patrick's Roman Catholic Church in Miami Beach.

A lone gunman shot Versace twice in the head outside his Spanish-style mansion on Miami Beach's Ocean Drive as he strolled home from a cafe after buying magazines on Tuesday morning. The death of the man who dressed stars and royalty caused an outpouring of grief worldwide.
Versace was a leading light of Miami Beach, a trendy area of night clubs, cafes, model agencies and Art Deco hotels popular with fun-seekers and home to a large gay community.

The family asked for donations to be sent to two of Versace's favourite charities instead of flowers -- the Elton John Aids Foundation and the Sting Rainforest Foundation. Both rock stars are among the luminaries he dressed.
